q: A server has one public HTTPS port, and you run a web app and an API as two programs. How can both answer on that one port?
options: Each app must have its own public port, and the browser must know both
One reverse proxy owns the port and passes each request to the right app by host and path
The two apps share the port by taking turns
Docker opens the port twice
why: Only one program can listen on a port. A reverse proxy such as nginx owns the front door, reads the host and the path of each request, and passes it to an app behind it. The browser only knows the proxy.

q: nginx has two server blocks, shop.example.test first and admin.example.test second. A request arrives with Host: other.test. What happens?
options: nginx answers 404 at once
nginx refuses the connection
The first server block answers, because it is the default server for the port
The second server block answers, because it is the last one
why: When no server_name matches, nginx uses the default server for that port, which is the first one unless you mark another. In the real run, other.test got the shop home page.

q: A pool has app1 and app2. app1 is stopped and app2 runs. What status do users get?
options: 502 for every second request
502 for every request until app1 returns
200 for every request, because nginx tries the next app for the same request
504 after 60 seconds
why: A refused connection makes nginx try the next app in the pool for the same request, so users see no error. The nginx log shows the refused connection. The cost is that app2 now carries all the work.

q: Both apps were down and gave 502. You start them again. What do users get at once?
options: 200 at once, because the apps are up
502 can last about 10 seconds, because nginx rests a failed app for fail_timeout (10 seconds by default)
504 for 60 seconds
A 404 until you restart nginx
why: nginx marks a failed app as down and leaves it alone for fail_timeout, 10 seconds by default. In the real run the answers were 502 until about 10 seconds after the apps were back, and then 200. The app is up before nginx knows it is up.

q: Your Express app sits behind nginx and you set nothing else. What does req.ip show, and what fixes it?
options: The real client address, always
nginx's address. Set X-Forwarded-For in nginx and trust proxy in Express
No address, because proxies hide it
The address of the database
why: The app talks to nginx, not to the browser, so by default it sees nginx as the sender (Express derives the address from the socket). Set proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for in nginx, and set trust proxy in Express so it reads the list from the right.

q: In CapRover, where does HTTPS end, and what does your Node app speak behind it?
options: HTTPS ends in your Node app, which holds the certificate
HTTPS ends in nginx, and your app speaks plain HTTP behind it
HTTPS ends in the database
HTTPS is not used in CapRover
why: CapRover runs nginx as a reverse proxy in front of each app. TLS terminates in nginx, with a certificate from Let's Encrypt, and the Swarm service speaks plain HTTP. This is the same idea as an ingress controller in Kubernetes.
